name: IT Domain Readiness Assessment
source_name: Team-written items; skills mapped to O*NET 31.0, references cited per item
disclaimer: An indicative self-check of job-entry skills, not a certification or a hiring decision.
exams_note: Each question may name the certification exam section that covers the same topic. Team mapping by exam section, read off the official syllabus or exam objectives on 2026-10-31; not endorsed by the exam owners. Security+ V8 is due around 2026-11-17, so recheck SY0-701 then.

sections.2: Control Flow: Conditional Blocks and Loops
sections.3: Data Collections: Tuples, Dictionaries, Lists, and Strings

sections.2: Testing Throughout the Software Development Lifecycle

review.note: Raise these when outside experts have reviewed the bank and students have piloted it; the results page shows them.

selection.note: Stage 1: 3 random quick-check items in each tested area (3-6 areas chosen from the CV and interests; all 6 when neither is given), giving every tested area the same chance. Stage 2: in the 2 tested areas with the most quick-check points (ties broken by the seed), 2 deep items and 1 hands-on item each (6). 15 items for 3 areas, 24 for 6.

scoring.partial_credit: code: points x tests passed / tests; multi: points x max(0, correct picks - wrong picks) / correct options; others all-or-nothing
scoring.text: correct when the trimmed, lower-cased answer with spaces removed equals one of accept
scoring.code: run in the browser (Pyodide in a Web Worker, 5 s limit); outputs are compared after a JSON round trip, so tuples equal lists
scoring.sql: run setup_sql then the answer in an in-memory SQLite database; rows compared in order with numbers rounded to 2 decimals
scoring.domain_readiness: deep + practical points earned / possible for that domain, as 0-100
scoring.area_profile: quick-check points / possible for every area, as 0-100; ranks all 6 areas

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.code:
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1)
print(add(2))
questions.explanation: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call shares the same list.

refs.name: Python FAQ: Why are default values shared between objects?

questions.prompt: A function checks whether a list of n integers contains a duplicate by comparing every pair (O(n^2)). Which rewrite runs in O(n) on average?
options: Sort the list, then compare neighbours
Walk the list once, keeping seen values in a hash set
Binary-search the list for each element
questions.explanation: Hash-set membership is O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n). Sorting first is O(n log n); binary search needs a sorted list and is also O(n log n).

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare floats with math.isclose().

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: b = a does not copy the list; both names point to the same list object.

refs.name: Python FAQ: How do I copy an object?

questions.prompt: A unit test for checkout() calls the real payment gateway and fails whenever the network is slow. What is the best fix?
options: Retry the test up to 5 times
Replace the gateway with a mock or stub in the unit test
Run the tests only at night
questions.explanation: Unit tests should not depend on outside services. A mock makes the test fast and repeatable; the real gateway belongs in a separate integration test.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.code:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])
questions.explanation: Each lambda looks up i when it is called, not when it is created. By then the loop has finished and i is 2.

refs.name: Python FAQ: Why do lambdas defined in a loop all return the same result?

questions.prompt: You committed a database password to a feature branch and already pushed it to the shared remote. What is the correct FIRST step?
options: Run git revert on the commit and push again
Revoke or rotate the password, then clean it out of the history
Amend the commit and force-push the branch
Delete the feature branch on the remote
questions.explanation: Anyone who fetched the branch already has the password, and rewriting history does not remove their copies. Treat it as leaked: rotate it first, then remove it from the history.

refs.name: GitHub Docs: Removing sensitive data from a repository

questions.prompt: A ReportExporter class has an if/elif chain on format ("pdf", "xlsx", ...). Every new format means editing and re-testing this class. Which principle does this most directly break?
questions.explanation: Open/Closed: code should be open for extension (add a new exporter) but closed for modification (no edits to existing, tested code).

questions.prompt: is_leap(year) should follow the Gregorian rule: divisible by 4, except centuries, unless divisible by 400. Which set of test years is most likely to catch a wrong implementation?
questions.explanation: It covers one case for each branch of the rule: an ordinary leap year, a non-leap year, a century that is not leap (1900) and a century that is (2000).

questions.prompt: Binary search on a sorted list of 1,000 distinct numbers: what is the maximum number of probes (elements checked) needed to find a value or decide it is missing?
questions.explanation: Each probe halves the range: floor(log2(1000)) + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run `counter += 1` 100,000 times on a shared global, with no lock. What can you say about the final value?
options: It is always 200,000 because Python has a GIL
It can be less than 200,000 because += is a read-modify-write, not one atomic step
Python raises an error for unsynchronised writes
questions.explanation: The GIL lets only one thread run bytecode at a time, but a thread can be switched out between reading counter and writing it back, so updates can be lost. Use a threading.Lock.

questions.prompt: Write merge_intervals(intervals). It takes a list of [start, end] pairs (start <= end, any order) and returns the overlapping or touching intervals merged, sorted by start. [1, 4] and [4, 5] touch, so they merge to [1, 5].

    # return: list of [start, end], merged and sorted
    pass
questions.explanation: Sort by start, then extend the last merged interval while the next start is <= its end.

questions.prompt: Write is_balanced(s). Return True if every bracket in s, (), [] and {}, is closed by the matching type in the right order. Other characters are ignored.
questions.explanation: Push each opening bracket on a stack; each closing bracket must match the top. The stack must be empty at the end.

refs.name: Python docs: Using lists as stacks

questions.prompt: Table orders(customer_id, amount). Which query lists customers whose total spend is above 1000?
options: SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE SUM(amount) > 1000;
SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000;
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE amount > 1000 GROUP BY customer_id;
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY amount > 1000;
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.prompt: A fraud model scores 99% accuracy on data where 1% of transactions are fraud. What is the main concern?
options: Predicting 'not fraud' for everything also scores 99%, so check precision and recall on the fraud class
Accuracy should be computed on the training set
questions.explanation: On imbalanced data accuracy hides failure on the rare class. Recall shows how many frauds are caught.

questions.prompt: In a survey of fresh graduates, the mean monthly salary is RM 12,000 but the median is RM 4,500. What does this most likely mean?
options: A few very high salaries pull the mean up (right-skewed data)
The median is always lower than the mean
questions.explanation: The median is resistant to extreme values; a mean far above it signals a long right tail. Report the median for typical pay.

refs.name: OpenStax Introductory Statistics: Skewness and the mean, median and mode

questions.prompt: An orders table repeats each customer's full address in every order row. A customer moves house. What problem does this design cause?
options: The address must be updated in many rows, and missed rows leave inconsistent data
The table cannot have a primary key
questions.explanation: This is an update anomaly. Normalise: keep the address once in a customers table and reference it by customer_id.

questions.prompt: Which task is unsupervised learning?
options: Predicting house prices from past sales
Grouping customers into segments when no labels exist
Classifying emails as spam or not spam from labelled examples
Predicting exam scores from study hours
questions.explanation: Clustering finds structure without labels. The other tasks learn from known answers, which is supervised learning.

questions.prompt: A classifier gives TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 60, TN = 890. What is its recall? (decimal, e.g. 0.75)
questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 100 = 0.4. (Precision would be 40 / 50 = 0.8.)

questions.prompt: A churn model predicts whether a customer will leave next month. It reaches 98% AUC in testing but fails in production. Which input feature is the most likely cause?
options: Number of support tickets last quarter
questions.explanation: account_closed_date is only known after the customer has churned, so it leaks the answer during training and is missing at prediction time.

questions.prompt: Training accuracy is 99% but validation accuracy is 70%. Which action is most likely to help?
options: Add regularisation or reduce model complexity
questions.explanation: A large train/validation gap means overfitting. Regularisation, a simpler model or more data narrows it.

questions.prompt: Which query returns customers who have NEVER placed an order?
options: SELECT c.id FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id = NULL;
SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.id IS NULL;
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps customers without orders, with NULL order columns. `= NULL` is never true; an inner JOIN drops them; moving the test into ON returns every customer.

questions.prompt: Table t has one column x with the values 1, 2, NULL, 4. What does SELECT AVG(x) FROM t; return? (2 decimal places)
questions.explanation: Aggregates skip NULL: (1 + 2 + 4) / 3 = 2.33, not 7 / 4.

questions.prompt: An HR chatbot built on an LLM invents company leave policies that do not exist. What is the most effective fix?
options: Retrieve the real policy documents and have the model answer from them, citing sources (RAG)
Add 'do not lie' to the prompt
Fine-tune it on random internet text
questions.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in your own documents and lets users check the cited source.

refs.name: Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

questions.prompt: Write top_categories(rows, n). rows is a list of [category, amount]; amount may be None (skip that row). Return the n categories with the highest total as a list of [category, total] with total rounded to 2 decimals, sorted by total (highest first), then category name (A-Z).
questions.explanation: Sum into a dict, skipping None; sort items with key (-total, name); round; slice to n.

refs.name: Python docs: Sorting HOW TO (key functions)

questions.prompt: Write one SQL query (SQLite). Using only orders dated in 2025, list each customer's name and total spend as columns name, total, for customers with at least 2 orders in 2025, highest total first.
questions.explanation: JOIN customers to orders, filter order_date to 2025 in WHERE, GROUP BY customer, HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2, ORDER BY total DESC. Mei Ling's 2024 order must not count.

questions.prompt: A login check builds its SQL like this. What is the right fix?
questions.code: sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "' AND pw_hash = '" + h + "'"
options: Strip single quotes from name before building the string
Use a parameterised query with placeholders
Hide database error messages from the user
Validate the name field with JavaScript in the browser
questions.explanation: Parameterised queries keep data separate from SQL code. Stripping characters is easy to bypass and browser checks can be skipped.

refs.name: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

questions.prompt: How should a new web app store user passwords?
options: AES-encrypted, with the key in the config file
Argon2id or bcrypt, with a unique salt per password
questions.explanation: Password hashing functions such as Argon2id and bcrypt are deliberately slow and salted, so cracking stolen hashes is expensive. Fast hashes and reversible encryption are not suitable.

questions.prompt: An email from security@mayb4nk-support.com says your account is locked and asks you to log in through its link within 1 hour. What do you do?
options: Click the link quickly before the account is closed
Reply asking whether it is real
Do not click; report it, and check by typing the bank's official address yourself
Forward it to friends to warn them
questions.explanation: Look-alike domain, urgency and a login link are classic phishing signs. Use a channel you trust, not anything in the email.

questions.prompt: What does multi-factor authentication (MFA) protect against best?
options: Malware already running on the server
An attacker logging in with a stolen or guessed password
questions.explanation: With MFA the password alone is not enough; the attacker also needs the second factor.

questions.prompt: A website shows the HTTPS padlock. What does that tell you?
options: The site is safe and run by an honest company
The connection to that domain is encrypted, nothing more
Your password is stored securely by the site
questions.explanation: TLS protects data in transit to the named domain. Phishing sites routinely have valid certificates.

questions.prompt: You see these lines in /var/log/auth.log on a public server. What happened, and what do you do?
questions.code:
Oct 23 10:01:02 web01 sshd[811]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.5 port 52011 ssh2
Oct 23 10:01:03 web01 sshd[811]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.5 port 52013 ssh2
... 412 more failed attempts from 203.0.113.5 ...
Oct 23 10:09:41 web01 sshd[811]: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.5 port 53990 ssh2
options: A port scan; no action because it was only probing
A successful brute-force login as root; treat the server as compromised and start incident response
A user who forgot the password; reset it
questions.explanation: Hundreds of failures followed by a success from the same address is a successful password-guessing attack. Isolate the host, preserve logs, and then disable password and root logins.

questions.prompt: A comment box shows comments with the code below. A user posts . What is the best fix?
options: Set commentDiv.textContent instead, or encode the output for HTML
Only allow logged-in users to comment
Move the code into a separate .js file
questions.explanation: The payload has no <script> tag, so keyword filters miss it. textContent treats the input as text, never as HTML.

refs.name: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

questions.prompt: Ransomware encrypts a clinic's patient files and the attackers threaten to publish a copy. Which security properties are hit?
questions.explanation: Encrypted files cannot be used (availability), and the stolen copy is exposed (confidentiality).

refs.name: NIST CSRC glossary: confidentiality, integrity, availability

questions.prompt: An API accepts a JWT whose header says {"alg": "none"} and has an empty signature. What is the impact and fix?
options: None; the payload is still Base64-encoded
Anyone can forge a token for any user; the server must allow only its expected algorithm and always verify the signature
Tokens expire too quickly; raise the exp claim
The token is too long; switch to cookies
questions.explanation: Without signature verification the claims, including the user id and role, are whatever the attacker writes.

refs.name: RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

questions.prompt: EDR shows one staff laptop beaconing to a known command-and-control server after a phishing email. What is the best NEXT step?
options: Wipe and reinstall the laptop immediately
Isolate the laptop from the network while keeping it powered on for evidence
Shut down the whole office network
Email all staff about the phishing first
questions.explanation: Containment comes first, and isolating rather than wiping keeps memory and disk evidence so you can find out what else was touched.

questions.prompt: GET /api/invoices/1043 shows your invoice. Changing it to /api/invoices/1044 shows another customer's invoice. What is this, and what fixes it?
options: Broken access control (IDOR); check on the server that the invoice belongs to the logged-in user
Cross-site request forgery; add a CSRF token
questions.explanation: The server trusts the id in the URL. Every request must be authorised against the current user; random ids alone only hide the problem.

refs.name: OWASP Insecure Direct Object Reference Prevention Cheat Sheet

questions.prompt: A bank moves money with GET /transfer?to=ACC&amount=500, authenticated only by the session cookie. An attacker's page contains . What is this, and what fixes it?
options: CSRF; use POST with a CSRF token and SameSite cookies
Clickjacking; add a CAPTCHA to the image
questions.explanation: The victim's browser sends the cookie automatically. State changes must not use GET, and need a token the attacker's page cannot read.

questions.prompt: A port scan of your public web server shows this. Which finding is the most urgent?
questions.code:
PORT     STATE SERVICE
22/tcp   open  ssh
80/tcp   open  http
443/tcp  open  https
3306/tcp open  mysql
options: The MySQL database (3306) is reachable from the internet
SSH on 22 should move to another port
questions.explanation: A database should only be reachable from the app servers. Exposing it invites password guessing and exploits; firewall it to the private network.

questions.prompt: In a Wireshark capture on the campus Wi-Fi you can read this request in plain text. What is the root problem and fix?
questions.code:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: portal.example.edu.my
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=aiman&password=Kopi%40123
options: The password is too weak; force longer passwords
The login uses HTTP, not HTTPS; serve it over TLS and enable HSTS
The username should be hashed in the browser
questions.explanation: Anyone on the network can read unencrypted HTTP. TLS encrypts the request; HSTS stops browsers from falling back to HTTP.

Count the lines containing "Failed password" per source IP; the IP is the word after the LAST " from " in the line (a username can itself be "from"). Return the IPs with at least threshold failures, sorted by count (highest first), then by IP as a string (ascending).

questions.prompt: Select EVERY line that is a path traversal attempt (trying to reach files outside the web folder).
questions.code:
1  198.51.100.7   GET /index.html                                   200
2  198.51.100.7   GET /download?file=../../etc/passwd                400
3  203.0.113.9    GET /download?file=report.pdf                      200
4  203.0.113.9    GET /download?file=%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd  200

    pass
questions.explanation: Hash each word once into a dict {digest: word}, then look up every user's hash. Without salts one wordlist pass cracks every user at once.

questions.prompt: After `chmod 640 secrets.env`, who can do what?
options: Everyone can read; only the owner can write
Owner can read and write; group can read; others have no access
Owner can read, write and execute; group can read
Owner and group can read and write; others can read
questions.explanation: 6 = rw- (owner), 4 = r-- (group), 0 = --- (others).

questions.prompt: A stateless web app slows down every evening at peak load and is fine the rest of the day. What is the best cloud approach?
options: Buy the largest VM and run it all day
Run several instances behind a load balancer with auto scaling on load
Move the database onto the web server
questions.explanation: Stateless apps scale out easily; auto scaling adds instances at peak and removes them afterwards, so you only pay for what you use.

questions.prompt: You rent a virtual machine in the cloud and must install and patch its operating system yourself. Which service model is this?
questions.explanation: Infrastructure as a Service gives you the VM; you manage everything from the OS up. PaaS and SaaS manage the OS for you.

refs.name: NIST SP 800-145: The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing

questions.prompt: How many usable host addresses are in an IPv4 /27 subnet?
questions.explanation: 32 - 27 = 5 host bits, 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses = 30.

questions.prompt: A user can ping 1.1.1.1 but no website opens by name (for example, www.mohe.gov.my). What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Reaching an internet IP proves the cable, IP settings and gateway work. Failing only by name points to DNS.

refs.name: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

questions.prompt: With this Dockerfile, every small code change reinstalls all dependencies and the build takes 5 minutes. What fixes it?
questions.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "/app/main.py"]
options: Copy requirements.txt and run pip install first, then COPY the rest of the code
Put everything in one RUN line
questions.explanation: Docker reuses a cached layer until one of its inputs changes. Copying only requirements.txt first means code changes no longer invalidate the pip layer.

questions.prompt: When does the cron entry `30 2 * * 1 /opt/backup.sh` run?
options: On the 2nd of every month at 00:30
questions.explanation: Fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week: minute 30, hour 2, any day, any month, weekday 1 (Monday).

questions.prompt: A service promises 99.9% availability over a 30-day month. How many minutes of downtime does that allow?
questions.explanation: 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes.

questions.prompt: A CI pipeline only needs to upload build files to one storage bucket. Which permission should its credentials get?
options: Full access to all storage buckets
Write (put object) on that one bucket only
questions.explanation: Least privilege: if the CI secret leaks, the attacker can only write to one bucket.

refs.name: AWS IAM: Security best practices (least privilege)

questions.prompt: `df -h` shows / at 100%, but `du -sh /*` adds up to only 60% of the disk. You already deleted a 20 GB log file. What is the most likely explanation?
options: df is cached and will update tomorrow
A running process still holds the deleted log file open, so its space is not freed
du does not count files in /var
questions.explanation: A file's blocks are only freed when the last open handle closes. `lsof +L1` finds it; restart the process or truncate it via /proc.

questions.prompt: The business requires at most 15 minutes of data loss (RPO) and recovery within 1 hour (RTO). Today there is one nightly full backup on the same server. Which change meets both targets?
options: Move the nightly backup to another disk in the same server
Ship transaction logs to another region every 5 minutes and rehearse the restore regularly
Switch to weekly backups kept offsite
questions.explanation: Log shipping every 5 minutes keeps data loss under 15 minutes, a separate region survives the server's loss, and rehearsal proves the 1-hour RTO. RAID is not a backup.

refs.name: AWS Well-Architected: Reliability pillar (disaster recovery objectives)

questions.prompt: You must split 192.168.10.0/24 into as many equal subnets as possible, each with at least 50 usable hosts. Which subnet mask do you use? (dotted decimal, e.g. 255.255.255.0)
questions.explanation: 50 hosts need 6 host bits (62 usable), so the prefix is /26 = 255.255.255.192, giving 4 subnets.

questions.prompt: A host is 10.0.5.20/22. Which address is in the SAME subnet?
questions.explanation: A /22 block covers 4 values of the third octet. 5 falls in 4-7, so the subnet is 10.0.4.0 - 10.0.7.255.

questions.prompt: A new PC has a link light and the correct static IP, mask and gateway, but cannot ping the gateway. `arp -a` shows the gateway entry as incomplete. Where is the fault most likely?
options: Layer 2: the switch port is in the wrong VLAN
Layer 3: the ISP route is down
questions.explanation: The link is up (layer 1 works) but ARP gets no reply, so frames are not reaching the gateway's broadcast domain - typically a wrong access VLAN.

refs.name: RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol

questions.prompt: Why do voice and video calls usually run over UDP rather than TCP?
options: A late, retransmitted packet is useless for live audio, and TCP would stall waiting for it
UDP packets are always delivered in order
questions.explanation: TCP guarantees ordered delivery by retransmitting, which adds delay. Real-time media prefers to skip a lost packet.

refs.name: RFC 3550: RTP, A Transport Protocol for Real-Time Applications

questions.prompt: A web server's connection table is full. The firewall shows thousands of SYN packets from many source addresses, with no matching final ACK. What is this?
options: A TCP SYN flood (denial of service)
questions.explanation: Half-open handshakes fill the server's backlog. Mitigations include SYN cookies and upstream filtering.

refs.name: RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations

questions.prompt: A router has these routes. Which next hop does it use for a packet to 10.1.3.7?
questions.explanation: Longest prefix match: 10.1.2.0/24 does not contain 10.1.3.7, so the most specific match is 10.1.0.0/16 via R2.

refs.name: RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers (5.2.4.3)

questions.prompt: Write find_full_disks(df_text, threshold). df_text is the output of `df -h` (a header line, then one line per filesystem). Return the mount points whose Use% is at least threshold, sorted by Use% (highest first), then mount point (A-Z). A mount point can contain spaces.

tmpfs           3.9G     0  3.9G   0% /dev/shm

questions.prompt: Write availability(outages, period_minutes). outages is a list of [start, end] minutes; outages can overlap and can start before 0 or end after period_minutes (only the part inside [0, period_minutes] counts). Return the availability percentage rounded to 3 decimals.
questions.explanation: Clip each outage to the period, merge overlaps (do not double-count), sum the downtime, then 100 * (1 - down / period).

questions.prompt: Write network_address(ip, prefix) without the ipaddress module. ip is a dotted IPv4 string and prefix is 0-32. Return the network address as a dotted string.
questions.explanation: Turn the four octets into one 32-bit integer, AND it with a mask of prefix leading 1-bits, then split back into octets. Watch prefix 0.

questions.prompt: Plan 192.168.50.0/24 with VLSM, allocating the largest subnet first, each starting at the lowest free address: Sales needs 100 hosts, IT 50 hosts, HR 20 hosts, and a router link 2 hosts. What is HR's subnet? Answer as network/prefix, e.g. 10.0.0.0/24.
What colour is the heading?
questions.code:
Hello

h1.heading.big { color: blue; } #title { color: red; } h1 { color: green; }
questions.explanation: One id selector outranks any number of class selectors, so #title wins regardless of order.

questions.prompt: What is the best fix for this delete control?
options: Use <button type="button" aria-label="Delete"> with the icon inside
Add a title attribute to the img
questions.explanation: A div cannot be reached with the keyboard and has no accessible name. A real button is focusable and keyboard-operable; aria-label gives screen readers a name.

questions.prompt: Which element should wrap a site's main menu links?
questions.explanation: <nav> tells browsers and screen readers that this is navigation, so users can jump straight to it.

questions.prompt: On phones your responsive site shows the tiny, zoomed-out desktop layout, even though the CSS has media queries. What is most likely missing?
questions.explanation: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render at about 980 px wide and scale down, so the media queries never match.

questions.prompt: A registration form rejects a phone number. How should it show the error?
options: A red border on the field only
A message next to the field saying what is wrong and how to fix it, e.g. "Use digits only, like 0123456789"
Clear the whole form so the user starts again
questions.explanation: Errors should be specific, next to the field, and not rely on colour alone (WCAG 3.3.1, 3.3.3, 1.4.1).

questions.prompt: In what order are the letters logged?
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (A, D). Promise callbacks are microtasks and run before the next macrotask, the timer (C, then B).

questions.prompt: A logged-in user calls DELETE /api/users/7 but is not an admin. Which status code should the API return?
options: 404 Not Found is the only safe choice
questions.explanation: 401 means not authenticated. The user is authenticated but lacks permission, which is 403.

questions.prompt: A React app at http://localhost:3000 calls fetch('http://localhost:8000/api'). The browser console shows a CORS error. Where is the fix?
options: Add mode: 'no-cors' to the fetch call
Have the API server send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000 (and handle preflight)
Turn off the browser's security settings
questions.explanation: CORS is a permission the server grants. no-cors only gives you an opaque response you cannot read.

questions.prompt: Largest Contentful Paint is 6 s on mobile. The largest element is a 4 MB, 4000 px wide hero photo. What helps most?
options: Serve a resized, compressed image (e.g. AVIF/WebP with srcset) and preload it
questions.explanation: The LCP element itself is the bottleneck. Shrinking it and fetching it early speeds up LCP; lazy-loading the hero image makes it worse.

questions.prompt: Analytics show 40% of users abandon an 18-field checkout form. What is the best next step?
options: Change the button colour to red
Watch 5 users try the form, remove or defer non-essential fields, then measure again
Make every field required so data is complete
questions.explanation: Find the actual problem by observing users, fix it, and test again. Shorter forms reduce effort.

refs.name: ISO 9241-210: Human-centred design for interactive systems

questions.prompt: What is the minimum contrast ratio WCAG 2.2 level AA requires for normal-size body text?
questions.explanation: AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text; 7:1 is the AAA level.

questions.prompt: Write paginate(items, page, per_page). page starts at 1. Return a dict with keys items (that page's slice), page, total_pages, has_prev, has_next. Raise ValueError if per_page < 1 or page < 1, or if page > total_pages when there is at least one item. An empty list has total_pages 0 and page 1 is allowed.
questions.explanation: total_pages = ceil(len / per_page); validate first; slice items[(page-1)*per_page : page*per_page].

questions.prompt: Select EVERY line that fails WCAG 2.2 level AA.
questions.code:
1 2 3
Save
4 5 Download annual report (PDF) 6

Terms and conditions apply
questions.explanation: 1: no alt text. 3: a div is not keyboard-operable. 4: a placeholder is not a label. 6: #999 on white is about 2.85:1, below 4.5:1. Lines 2 and 5 are fine.

questions.prompt: In Scrum, who decides the order of items in the Product Backlog?
questions.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog to maximise value.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a NON-functional requirement?
options: Students can download their transcript as PDF
Search results appear within 2 seconds for 95% of requests
Lecturers can enter marks for each assignment
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as performance, security and availability, not features.

questions.prompt: Halfway through a fixed-price project, the client keeps asking for "small" extra features but the deadline and budget stay the same. What is this, and what should the project manager do?
options: Normal agile work; just add them
Scope creep; route each request through change control and agree the impact on time and cost
Gold plating; refuse to talk to the client
Risk acceptance; ask the team to work weekends
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled additions are scope creep. A change-control process makes the trade-off visible before work starts.

questions.prompt: Which tool shows task dependencies and lets you find the critical path?
questions.explanation: A network diagram links each task to the ones it depends on; the longest path through it is the critical path.

questions.prompt: Staff are resisting a new HR system that goes live next month. What is the best first step?
options: Make it compulsory and switch off the old system early
Involve key users: explain why it changes, train them and act on their feedback
Delay the launch by a year
questions.explanation: People adopt systems they understand and helped shape. Communication, training and listening reduce resistance.

questions.prompt: A project has Planned Value RM 80,000, Earned Value RM 60,000 and Actual Cost RM 75,000. What is its Cost Performance Index (CPI)? (2 decimal places)
questions.explanation: CPI = EV / AC = 60,000 / 75,000 = 0.80: every ringgit spent delivers 80 sen of planned work.

questions.prompt: PV = RM 50,000, EV = RM 55,000, AC = RM 60,000. What is the project's status?
options: Ahead of schedule but over budget
Ahead of schedule and under budget
questions.explanation: SPI = EV / PV = 1.10 (ahead of schedule). CPI = EV / AC = 0.92 (over budget).

questions.prompt: The only developer who knows the payment module might leave mid-project (medium probability, high impact). Which response is best?
options: Mitigate: pair programming, documentation and cross-training
Avoid it by cancelling the project
questions.explanation: Mitigation lowers the impact if the risk happens. Cancelling is out of proportion, and insurance does not replace knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which project suits a predictive (waterfall) approach best?
options: A start-up app whose features depend on user feedback
A system for a legally fixed tax rule, with complete requirements and a fixed-price government contract
A research prototype exploring new AI ideas
A marketing website that changes weekly
questions.explanation: Waterfall works when requirements are stable and well understood up front. Uncertain or changing products fit agile better.

questions.prompt: A student can enrol in many courses and a course has many students. How do you model this in a relational database?
options: Put a course_id column in the students table
Put a list of student ids in one column of courses
Create an enrolments table with student_id and course_id foreign keys
Merge students and courses into one table
questions.explanation: A many-to-many relationship needs a junction (associative) table; it can also hold enrolment data such as the grade.

questions.prompt: A team completes 30 story points per 2-week sprint on average. 210 points remain in the backlog. How many weeks until it is done, at this pace?
questions.explanation: 210 / 30 = 7 sprints x 2 weeks = 14 weeks. (A real forecast would give a range, since velocity varies.)

questions.prompt: What is the shortest possible duration of this project, in days?
questions.code:
Task  Days  Depends on
A     3     -
B     5     A
C     2     A
D     4     C
E     3     B, D
F     2     A
questions.explanation: Paths: A-B-E = 11, A-C-D-E = 12, A-F = 5. The critical path A-C-D-E takes 12 days; B has 1 day of float.

questions.prompt: These requirements are for a university assignment portal. Select EVERY non-functional requirement.
questions.code:
1  Students can submit an assignment before its deadline.
2  Pages load in under 2 seconds on a 4G connection.
3  Student data is stored in Malaysia to comply with the PDPA.
4  Lecturers can export marks as a CSV file.
5  The portal is available 99.5% of the time during semester.
6  Students receive an email when a mark is released.
7  Passwords are stored as salted bcrypt hashes.
8  The interface meets WCAG 2.2 level AA.
questions.explanation: Lines 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8 set qualities or constraints (performance, compliance, availability, security, accessibility). Lines 1, 4 and 6 are features.
